title: Younès Rabii-There’s A Skull In My Garden: Simple interactions give new meanings to generated things
speaker: Younès Rabii-There’s A Skull In My Garden
talk_title: Simple interactions give new meanings to generated things
description:
This talk is from the 2020 virtual Roguelike Celebration:
https://roguelike.club/event2020.html

Younès is a PhD student exploring how generative AI and PCG techniques can be used to create whole new kinds of game experience. In this lightning talk he discusses surprising emergent phenomena they encountered when designing a simple game containing items with generated visuals. This explains how very simple game mechanics (eg: carrying an item) and generative system (eg: generating a symmetric image) can interact to create a context where players give their own meaning to found artifacts (eg: is that a cowboy hat on my head ? or from the title : There's A Skull in My Garden)

Find him on Twitter: https://twitter.com/Pyrofoux
Max Kreminski's talk on gardening as a mode of play: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TvlZinAvpwg&t=3s

segments.text: Hi everyone, I'm Younès Rabii I've been a game dev for the past 5 years and I'm also
a new phd student in game and AI and today i'd like to tell you about how simple interactions
can give new meanings to generated things or "There's A Skull In My Garden"
Let's delve into the what, why, and how of this project I'm going to tell you about
the way players can attach more meaning to generated things and it's important for us
because it's at the heart of what we like in rogue like and i'm going to explore
that with you by using the observations i made while designing a roguelike myself
So what's player interpretation well in the 20th century people used to play games
in what was called console mods where instead of the fancy new graphics that you have today
they used to represent things on screen with keyboard characters
so a thing like on the screen that looks like an ampy with a slash and a green 'g' letter
will be interpreted by the player as "I'm holding a sword and five
meters to the right there's a goblin" this step is what i call Player Interpretation
and Player Interpretation is actually very important for roguelike players and game
devs um because it it helps us going from the screenshots of dwarf fortress
that looks like someone just smashed their keyboard to whole stories with drama, with funny
moments, with plot twists and everything and the key to do that is Player Interpretation on what's
happening on screen and we care a lot about these stories we love them they are dear, to us and we
love them so much that we made a whole conference about about them so Player Interpretation is
actually very important you can also see designing roguelikes as shaping player interpretation
let's see how we can do that a bit so i'm going to speak about tea garden which is a
little roguelike that i started after watching Max Kreminsky talk in Roguelike Celebration
last year it was my attempt to make a gardening roguelike not just in the theme of the game but
in the way it is played. the gameplay loop is very simple you can brew tea and this tea can give you
dreams and in your dreams you can collect, you can see strange flowers which are generated by
the game and you can bring back to the real world the flowers that you liked
and the recipe to create a flower in the game is actually very very simple
you just take a six by six pixel grid you put some symmetry on it, horizontal symmetry,
diagonal symmetry ,everything and you color this pattern with at most two colors
since this is a pico 8 game this means that the colors i use are always
balanced they are already, they already match well together
so the visuals they are strange but sometimes they seem compelling and some players
give meaning to them even though the games the game doesn't attach one explicitly
and for instance this orange thing is just like an orange thing but this pink one looks kinda
like a butterfly and the green one looks like a frog face it's a bit like looking at clouds like
approximately 90% of the things you see is junk is it has no perceived meaning
whatsoever to any player but in the in the last 10 persons you can actually see things
that appeal to you and the more you you can recognize them the more you are attached to them
for instance i'm a pretty fan of this frog face myself it's round it's lovable it's previous to me
and these notions they are very different from player to player
but they can also be influenced by the game here's an example when i designed the game i added a new
interaction to it it was picking up something and since the character has no arms whatsoever
they just put objects on their heads and suddenly what happened is that flowers that had no meaning
before starting being seen as hats by players like this orange thing became cowboy hats
and suddenly it became their favorite flower - player interaction can help
can help meaningless visuals becoming something that holds a genuine meaning to the player
another example because you can pick up things you can also place them on ground
and suddenly it gave the player the ability to create arrangement of things and to to
to see in flowers things that could be arranged for instance since letters come from words the
player began to see some flowers as a letter a thing that they did not do before
what happens i think it is still my personal theory
is that actually the game creates a language with you the player and you you play an actual role
into creating this language even if you don't - even if you're not conscious about it for instance
the game tells you that something is pink and you tell yourself oh something that looks like this
it should be... and you're feeling the blank yourself here it could be a butterfly but
by adding a new interaction you're actually giving more opportunities to a player to
to fill in more blanks and give more meaning to what's in the game for instance here's something
that i can put on my head well it must be a hat or a crown or a helmet or something
that means that an interaction in the game can have a lot of impacts on player interpretation
and therefore the stories they create together what's interesting is that it can actually go
the other way too here's an example for instance um i know that i can wear a hat in the game but
sometimes i look at things and i see a mask in them and maybe i'd like to wear them too
but it's not a thing that i can do in the game but since i'm the developer i just
implant implemented this functionality because i wanted it it was organically natural for me
the interpretation i had influenced my desire for new interactions and what's cool is that
since we saw it before new interactions can help create new interpretations it's it's like a loop
that creates more and more meaning into the game and it means that not only player interpretation
has a role into how we give meaning to games but it also has a role into how we make games
or how we mod games or how we customize them too but you must be cautious because
it's very cool to to be able to evoke meaningful concepts to a player and they can be very powerful
but you cannot control them - they can be very positive like for instance these flowers that
is shaped like a little T and it's blue and pink and which i gave myself the meaning of
trans rights activism and it's very positive and it's very strong it's embedded in the real world but
i also came across flowers that were like crosses with four branches and it looked
to me like fascist imagery and it was not something that had wanted to to be in my game
you have to ask yourself is it something that you want to put to to be able to evoke
in your game and there's no easy solution to prevent that also there's something very very
fearsome with these concepts: it can spook the game dev one day i just wandered in into one
of my generated gardens for debugging purposes and i just came across a skull my own game spooked
me very scary well thank you thanks a lot for listening to my talk if you have any questions
or if you like to discuss it with me just reach me out on twitter thank you a lot for being there
